Using expsmooth: worked examples

Justin Carmody, Rob J Hyndman

21 November 2026

Source: vignettes/expsmooth-vignette.Rmd
expsmooth-vignette.Rmd

Introduction

This package contains a collection of data sets that are designed to accompany the book Forecasting with Exponential Smoothing: The State Space Approach by Rob J. Hyndman, Anne B. Koehler, J. Keith Ord, and Ralph D. Snyder (Springer, 2008).

When the expsmooth package is loaded, the forecast package is also loaded, providing the functions to fit and forecast with exponential smoothing state space models. We also use ggplot2 and patchwork for the graphs.

library(expsmooth)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

This vignette follows the analysis in Section 2.8 of the book, and provides worked solutions to Exercises 2.3 and 2.4. The forecast package has been updated since the book was published, so some of the resulting models and estimates differ from those in the book. Figure numbers are taken from the book.

Data sets

Chapters 1 and 2 use four data sets that are included in the expsmooth package.

  • bonds: 125 monthly US government bond yields (percent per annum) from January 1994 to May 2004.
  • usnetelec: 55 observations of annual US net electricity generation (billion kWh) for 1949 through 2003.
  • ukcars: 113 quarterly observations of passenger motor vehicle production in the UK (thousands of cars) for the first quarter of 1977 through the first quarter of 2005.
  • visitors: 240 monthly observations of the number of short-term overseas visitors to Australia from May 1985 to April 2005.

These time series are shown in Figure 1.1, which is reproduced below.

plot_bonds <- autoplot(bonds) +
  labs(
    title = "(a) US 10-year bond yields",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Percentage per annum"
  )
plot_usnetelec <- autoplot(usnetelec) +
  labs(
    title = "(b) US net electricity generation",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Billion kWh"
  )
plot_ukcars <- autoplot(ukcars) +
  labs(
    title = "(c) UK passenger vehicle production",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Thousands of cars"
  )
plot_visitors <- autoplot(visitors) +
  labs(
    title = "(d) Overseas visitors to Australia",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Thousands of people"
  )
(plot_bonds | plot_usnetelec) /
  (plot_ukcars | plot_visitors)

Automatic model selection and forecasting

This part of the vignette follows the automatic forecasting procedure described in Section 2.8 of the book. The book selected ETS(A,Ad,N) for bonds, ETS(M,Md,N) for usnetelec, ETS(A,N,A) for ukcars and ETS(M,A,M) for visitors. The current version of the forecast package selects the same models for bonds, ukcars and visitors, but selects ETS(M,A,N) for usnetelec.

The estimation and model selection are performed by the ets() function and the forecasting is done by the forecast() function. These are both part of the forecast package. A basic introduction to using these functions is given in Sections 7.6 and 7.7 of Forecasting: Principles and Practice by Rob J Hyndman and George Athanasopoulos.

The automatic forecasting process will be carried out for each of the four data sets. The process will be explained for the first data set, and the main results will be reported for the others.

bonds

The ets() function fits all appropriate models (optimising parameters in each case), and then selects the best model according to the AICc. The AICc is the default information criterion; the AIC or BIC can be used instead via the ic argument. (The book used the AIC; for these four series the AIC and AICc select the same models.)

fit_bonds <- ets(bonds)
summary(fit_bonds)
#> ETS(A,Ad,N) 
#> 
#> Call:
#> ets(y = bonds)
#> 
#>   Smoothing parameters:
#>     alpha = 0.9999 
#>     beta  = 0.0954 
#>     phi   = 0.8026 
#> 
#>   Initial states:
#>     l = 5.3252 
#>     b = 0.5934 
#> 
#>   sigma:  0.2428
#> 
#>      AIC     AICc      BIC 
#> 256.5383 257.2502 273.5082 
#> 
#> Training set error measures:
#>                       ME      RMSE       MAE        MPE     MAPE      MASE
#> Training set -0.01622111 0.2378765 0.1969524 -0.3276314 3.611147 0.2440042
#>                   ACF1
#> Training set 0.1426552

The autoplot() function can then be used to show the observed series together with the estimated level and slope components over time.

autoplot(fit_bonds)

The forecast() function is used to produce point forecasts and prediction intervals. When the summary() function is called on the forecast object, it prints the model information along with the point forecasts and prediction intervals.

forecast_bonds <- forecast(fit_bonds, level = 80)
summary(forecast_bonds)
#> 
#> Forecast method: ETS(A,Ad,N)
#> 
#> Model Information:
#> ETS(A,Ad,N)

The autoplot() function can then be called on the forecast object to produce the graph shown in Figure 2.1.

autoplot(forecast_bonds) +
  labs(
    title = "US 10-year bond yields",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Percentage per annum",
    caption = "Fig. 2.1a"
  )

usnetelec

For the remaining series, we show the fitted model and the graph of the forecasts.

fit_usnetelec <- ets(usnetelec)
fit_usnetelec
#> ETS(M,A,N) 
#> 
#> Call:
#> ets(y = usnetelec)
#> 
#>   Smoothing parameters:
#>     alpha = 0.9999 
#>     beta  = 0.2191 
#> 
#>   Initial states:
#>     l = 254.9338 
#>     b = 38.3125 
#> 
#>   sigma:  0.0259
#> 
#>      AIC     AICc      BIC 
#> 634.0437 635.2682 644.0803
forecast_usnetelec <- forecast(fit_usnetelec, level = 80)
autoplot(forecast_usnetelec) +
  labs(
    title = "US net electricity generation",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Billion kWh",
    caption = "Fig. 2.1b"
  )

ukcars 

fit_ukcars <- ets(ukcars)
fit_ukcars

#> Call:
#> ets(y = ukcars)

#>     alpha = 0.6199 
#>     gamma = 1e-04 
#> 
#>   Initial states:
#>     l = 314.2568 
#>     s = -1.7579 -44.9601 21.1956 25.5223

forecast_ukcars <- forecast(fit_ukcars, level = 80)
autoplot(forecast_ukcars) +
  labs(
    title = "UK passenger motor vehicle production",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Thousands of cars",
    caption = "Fig. 2.1c"
  )
